claims.claim: The GDPR was adopted on 14 April 2016 and became effective on 25 May 2018.
claims.episode_span: The regulation took effect on 25 May 2018.
claims.supporting_quote: The European Parliament and Council of the European Union adopted the GDPR on 14 April 2016, to become effective on 25 May 2018.

claims.claim: GDPR violators can be fined up to 20 million euros or up to 4 percent of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is greater.
claims.episode_span: consent interfaces to avoid fines that could reach 4 percent of global turnover
claims.supporting_quote: violators of the GDPR may be fined up to €20 million or up to 4% of the annual worldwide turnover of the preceding financial year in case of an enterprise, whichever is greater

claims.claim: A 2020 study of consent pop-ups on the top 10,000 UK websites found dark patterns and implied consent ubiquitous, with only 11.8 percent of designs meeting minimal legal requirements.
claims.episode_span: The interfaces frequently presented “accept all” as the most prominent button while burying granular controls behind additional clicks.
claims.source_title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence - arXiv
claims.supporting_quote: We found that dark patterns and implied consent are ubiquitous; only 11.8% meet the minimal requirements that we set based on European law.

claims.claim: Websites adopted third-party consent management platforms to comply with the GDPR's consent requirements.
claims.episode_span: Many companies adopted off-the-shelf banner scripts from vendors such as OneTrust and Cookiebot
claims.source_title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence - arXiv
claims.supporting_quote: New consent management platforms (CMPs) have been introduced to the web to conform with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, particularly its requirements for consent when companies collect and process users' personal data.

claims.claim: The ePrivacy Regulation, proposed in 2017 to replace the 2002 ePrivacy Directive, never came into force after years of delay.
claims.episode_span: the ePrivacy Regulation, intended to replace the older cookie rules, has been delayed for years
claims.source_title: ePrivacy Regulation, but the fight for your privacy is far from over - European Digital Rights (EDRi)
claims.supporting_quote: In 2017, the European Commission proposed an update to the 2002 ePrivacy Directive – an important but now-outdated law from the early days of the internet.

claims.claim: European data-protection authorities have scrutinized 'consent or pay' models; the EDPB held in 2024 that confronting users only with a choice between consenting to behavioural-advertising processing and paying a fee will in most cases not produce valid consent.
claims.episode_span: This practice, still under active review by data-protection authorities, created a new tension between privacy and access.
claims.source_title: EDPB: 'Consent or Pay' models should offer real choice | European Data Protection Board
claims.supporting_quote: it will not be possible for them to comply with the requirements for valid consent, if they confront users only with a choice between consenting to processing of personal data for behavioural advertising purposes and paying a fee
